The next day he had come and had sat there for an hour, talking quietly with her. He strove to be as entertaining as possible, told her about the Swedish actors and about a concert that some Polish artists had given. He suggested that she hear the French singers at Tivoli, but she had no desire to. He was determined to speak about something that amused her, and it really did seem that he was having some success. She listened to him kindly, asked about one thing and another, and thanked him at parting for the visit. He left her with a feeling that his presence had at least not been unpleasant to her, and on the stairs he considered how soon he might come again.

He waited a fortnight. She was at home and received him with a couple of polite words, but it was impossible for him to read from her expression whether the sight of him was welcome or unwelcome to her. He had hoped to come a little closer to her this time, but in that he was disappointed. His attempts to awaken her interest in what was going on and in what people were occupied with at the time were met with such measured answers that he became afraid of boring her. Then he fell silent so that she might begin talking about something; but then she merely made a few remarks about the weather, which were followed by a painful pause. He turned the conversation to the theater, but when she replied that she never went there and therefore had no interest in it,

20*

his courage sank. What could he possibly think of when faced with this hidden and closed-off woman? He left her with a melancholy feeling that he stood farther from her than ever before.—

When he was gone, Constance sat thinking how nice and agreeable he was. He gave an entirely different impression now than he had then; that was certain. Her aversion had disappeared, and deep down she felt a sort of fondness for him.

But even so, what did she want with his visits? She would rather do without them. It was too bothersome to sit there stiffly and have to answer and think of something to ask. And in general she did not like being disturbed when she sat occupied with her own thoughts. Why could they not leave her in peace?

She went out of the room and opened the kitchen door.

“Are you there, Johanne?” she asked.

Johanne demonstrated her presence by appearing in the doorway of the maid’s room.

“You recognize the gentleman you let in today, don’t you?”

“Doctor Lorck? Yes, goodness, of course.”

“If he comes again, I am not at home. Now do not forget that.”

“No, I shall be sure to remember,” said Johanne.

A month had passed, and in the course of it Lorck had tried in vain to see Constance three times. Then one day a letter came for her with the following contents:

Mrs. Constance Ring!

I have called on you several times without finding you at home; so I must try writing. But I am so afraid of offending or frightening you that I do not know how to couch my words. What I wish to tell you is that I have now pondered deeply over myself and you for a long time, and that I know in the depths of my soul that I love you with a love that would be worthy of you. With you lies happiness in life for me. If you will have nothing to do with me, I shall not find it on this earth.

If you could come to trust me, do you not think it might be possible for me, in time, to win your love?

Your most devoted,
Nils Lorck.

She was immensely surprised by his letter, but when she thought it over, it seemed to her so foolish that she had not understood before what he meant.

She replied at once:

Dear Dr. Lorck!

You must not be angry with me, but I do not think it is worthwhile for you to waste your time trying to win my love. It would be unworthy if, in order to obtain a little variety in my monotonous life, I began experimenting with myself and made use of you for that purpose. For it would be nothing else if I invited you to make a trial. I esteem you too highly for that, and I have not the slightest desire for it either. Do not think that I bear you any ill will; the opposite is the case. Of that you must be entirely convinced.

Yours,
Constance Ring.

NIRKAEEt

XXI.

About half a year had passed. Early in the winter, old District Judge Blom had died, and his wife had then gone to stay with her youngest daughter, who was married to a pastor at Nordfjordeidet. The childhood home had thus been broken up; the two brothers were each in his own place, and the other sister was living with her future parents-in-law in Molde.

Constance had been painfully affected by the news of her father’s death. It was as though the image of her happy childhood and early youth had perished at the same time. Now her dear father lay in the grave, and the other inhabitants of the beloved home were scattered to the four winds. There was no longer any fixed point to which she could attach her dreams and longings, no sheltered spot to which she could turn in thought in her most dejected moments. Everything had been swept away; she was so poor and bereft, her life so desolate and meaningless, and she often thought it would be best to die.—

At times she was also so sick and weary of it all that she seriously considered which method would be easiest when it came to taking her own life. But then evening and bedtime came, and then there was this: that she could lie down and sleep. It was a relief to sleep.

When she sat at home through the long, long afternoons—and she was always at home—it seemed to her that the hours would never end. Her loneliness tormented her, and yet the prospect of going out among people seemed to her even more dreadful.—

It was in March, a day of rough weather with northwesterly storm squalls, drenched in icy rawness. The remnants of the snow were dirty gray underneath, with brown patches here and there.

Constance had tried sewing for a while on an embroidered strip that always lay in the sewing basket. She had long since forgotten what she had originally intended to use it for. Then she had read a little, thrown down the book, paced the floor, and was now once more sewing a few stitches.
